subject: physics
title: Distance
summary: Distance is how much ground an object actually covers while moving — the length of its whole path, like a runner bag-tracking 400 m around a track. Distance is a plain number with no direction: it is always positive and only ever grows. Explore how tracking a path's length compares to the simpler straight-line jump of displacement.

compareCandidate.description: Both are measured here on the same map — distance is the total length of the winding path you walked (say 12 m), displacement is the straight line from your start to the stop (say 4 m). Distance never goes down.

plainLanguageExplanation: Distance is simply how far a journey goes — the full amount of ground covered, measured along the path you actually take. If you walk around a square, you add the length of each side: 10 m + 10 m + 10 m + 10 m = 40 m. That number, in meters, is the distance. It's a plain, directionless number — never negative — so it's called a scalar. The fun it is that distance is usually bigger than the straight-line hop between start and end, because going around streets or weaving through cones adds length. In this model you'll drag a character around an obstacle course, watch the distance counter climb, and compare it to the short straight arrow carried in the same frame. Distance gives us the meter-count we plug into speed = distance ÷ time, so it's the first truth about how much travel really happened.

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: The total length of the path an object travels, end to end

keyFacts.label: Unit
keyFacts.value: Meters (m) — bigger scales add kilometers, small ones centimeters

keyFacts.label: Scalar quantity
keyFacts.value: A plain number with no direction; it can never be negative or decrease

keyFacts.label: To measure
keyFacts.value: Add up every stretch of the path, whether straight, curved, or with turns

keyFacts.label: vs displacement
keyFacts.value: For a path with detours, distance is larger than the straight-line displacement

keyFacts.label: Speed link
keyFacts.value: Speed = distance ÷ time turns measured distance into how fast

whyItMatters: Distance powers almost every outdoor calculation in life: the length of a run, the fuel a car burns on a winding road, the drop a satellite covers around Earth. In physics, distance is the meter-scorer that speed and power are built on — and knowing whether someone is 'round' is how pilots and taxi drivers bill for the path actually traveled rather than the straight line on a map. Distance also sets the difference between covering ground and changing places, which is the key building block of the entire motion story.
tagline: How much ground did it cover?
didYouKnow: The word 'odometer' comes from the Greek words for 'path' and 'measure' — literally a path-measurer. A car's odometer counts distance (every bend), while a straight-line GPS shortcut can differ from it a lot — the same reason hiking trail signs read kilometers no one can rally with a ruler.
compareReason: The same path seen two ways — meters actually walked vs. the straight-line shortcut — is the clearest argument for why distance and displacement are different quantities.
